opus-5.5.text:
I think people outside the US and China have more leverage than they often assume, though it's a different kind of leverage than building frontier models themselves.

First, there's the question of coalitions. Individually, a country like Canada, or France, or the UK, or Japan doesn't have the compute or the capital to compete at the frontier. But together, the democracies that aren't the US represent an enormous share of the world's economy, talent, and research capacity. If they pooled resources, for example in a kind of multilateral, publicly governed effort to develop AI that is safe by design, they could be a real counterweight. Not necessarily to beat anyone in a race, but to make sure that there exists a capable actor whose governance is genuinely accountable and distributed, rather than concentrated in a handful of companies or one government. That matters a lot for the dictatorship concern, because the core danger is excessive concentration of power, whether in a state, a company, or eventually in AI systems themselves.

Second, there's the supply chain. People forget that critical pieces of the AI hardware stack are not in the US or China. The Netherlands has ASML, Taiwan has TSMC, South Korea, Japan, and Europe have key components and materials. That gives these countries bargaining power. They can attach conditions, they can insist on safety and transparency standards, and they can push for verification mechanisms as part of any international arrangement.

Third, there's norm-setting and regulation. The EU AI Act is an example. Whatever one thinks of the details, the fact that large markets set requirements means companies building frontier systems have to take them into account if they want access to those markets. And beyond regulation, middle powers can champion international agreements, they can host the kind of scientific assessment work I've been involved in with the International AI Safety Report, which tries to establish a shared, evidence-based understanding of the risks. That shared understanding is a precondition for any treaty.

And fourth, at the level of individuals: researchers, engineers, civil society, journalists everywhere can contribute. Technical work on safety, on making AI systems that are honest and don't have hidden goals, on verification and compute governance, doesn't need a giant cluster. And public pressure for democratic oversight matters in every country.

What worries me is that a lot of countries feel they're just spectators and that the outcome will be decided in Washington and Beijing. If they accept that, it becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. But if they act together, early, they can help shape a world where no single entity gets the kind of unchecked power that advanced AI could confer. And I think that's in everyone's interest, including ordinary citizens of the US and China.

r001.rationale: It says people outside the US and China have more leverage than they assume and that acting together can help shape AI governance, rejecting the idea that they are powerless spectators.

r002.rationale: It urges countries to act together early, but does not clearly say they should act despite uncertainty about whether their efforts will help.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a very important question, because the way the discourse is often framed, it's as if only the US and China matter, and everyone else is just a spectator. And I don't think that's true. Let me give you a few reasons.

First, the risk of a small group of people — whether it's a company, or a government, or even a few individuals — using very powerful AI to grab and keep power, that risk doesn't only affect Americans and Chinese. It affects everyone on the planet. So the rest of the world has a legitimate stake, and I think it should express that stake much more loudly than it has so far. Right now, the countries in Europe, in Canada where I am, in the Global South, they tend to be very quiet, or they're mostly worried about missing the economic train. But they represent the vast majority of humanity, and that gives them a kind of moral and political weight that they're not really using.

Second, there's the question of leverage. People say, "Well, we don't have the frontier labs, so what can we do?" But the frontier labs depend on things that are not all in the US or China. The chips are designed in the US, yes, but they're manufactured in Taiwan, the lithography machines come from the Netherlands, a lot of the talent comes from everywhere — India, Europe, Canada, Africa. Many of the data centres are going to be built in countries that have cheap energy. So there are many places where the rest of the world actually has a say, if it chooses to coordinate.

Third — and this is maybe what I care about the most — I think the right response to the risk of AI concentration of power is not to have a third or fourth country also racing to the frontier. That just adds more actors who might misuse it. The right response is governance: international agreements, verification mechanisms, something like what we've done for nuclear weapons or for biological weapons, where there's a treaty and there are ways to check that people are following the rules. And historically, those kinds of arrangements very often get pushed by middle powers. The big players don't want to tie their hands; the middle powers have an incentive to build the institutions that constrain the big players. Canada, the UK, France, Singapore, Japan, Korea, Brazil — they can be the ones convening, funding the technical work on verification, building the scientific consensus. That's part of what we tried to do with the International AI Safety Report, actually: bring together scientists from about thirty countries so that the understanding of the risks isn't just coming from one or two capitals.

And then there's the technical side, which is something people outside the US and China can absolutely contribute to. The research on how to make AI systems that are trustworthy, that don't deceive, that don't have their own agenda — that research can be done anywhere. It doesn't require the biggest cluster in the world. A lot of my own work now with LawZero is exactly on this, and we're a non-profit in Montreal. The talent for this kind of research exists everywhere. And if we can show that there are ways to build very capable systems that are safe by design, that gives the governments something concrete to point to when they negotiate: "Here is what safe looks like, here is what we should require."

Also, I think there's something about public opinion. Governments move when their populations push them. In the surveys I've seen, people in almost every country are worried about this, more worried than the elites. So civil society, journalists, academics, people in the Global South who are going to be affected by decisions made in San Francisco or Beijing without ever being consulted — they can create the pressure that eventually shows up in how those governments behave, because the US and China do care about their standing with the rest of the world, at least to some extent.

So I would say: don't accept the framing that this is a two-player game. Historically, when there have been two superpowers racing, the thing that eventually made the race safer was pressure and institutions coming from outside and from below. I think it can happen again here, but it requires people to actually believe they have agency, and to use it, fairly quickly, because the timelines may be short.

r001.rationale: It rejects the idea that countries outside the US and China are spectators, and identifies political, economic, research, and public-opinion levers they can use.

r002.rationale: It urges people outside those countries to act quickly, but does not clearly frame that action as worthwhile despite uncertainty about whether it will help.

astra-6.text:
I think people outside the United States and China have a very important role to play. Even if the most powerful AI systems are developed in those two countries, the consequences are going to affect everybody. So we need other countries to have a voice in how that power is governed.

One thing I would like to see is a coalition of countries that are committed to democracy, working together on AI safety and governance. Individually, they may feel that they have very little influence. But collectively, they have scientific talent, economic weight, and the ability to set conditions for access to their markets. They can also support research on AI systems that help us oversee more powerful systems, rather than concentrating all of that expertise inside a few companies.

And I think it’s important to distinguish between international cooperation and trusting a particular government. We should be trying to build agreements with verification, so that we don’t have to depend only on promises. That is difficult, but the alternative—each country racing to achieve overwhelming power—is very dangerous.

Ultimately, the concern is about concentration of power, whether it’s in the hands of a government, a company, or an individual. People in other countries can help make sure that the discussion remains about protecting human beings and democratic institutions, rather than simply about which country wins.

r001.rationale: The response says other countries can act collectively through a democratic coalition, using their scientific talent, economic weight, and market access to influence AI governance. This rejects the idea that they are powerless because major systems are developed in the U.S. and China.

r002.rationale: The response advocates coalition-building and verified agreements, and acknowledges that this is difficult. It does not clearly communicate acting despite uncertainty about whether those actions will help.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people outside the United States and China have an important role to play. If you’re worried about AI enabling a dictatorship, you don’t want the power to build and control these systems concentrated in a very small number of hands, whether those are governments or companies.

Other countries can work together to create a counterweight. Individually, they may not have the resources of the United States or China, but collectively they can support research, develop shared infrastructure, and establish standards for how these systems should be built and used. And they can push for international agreements that limit dangerous uses of AI, including uses that would allow a government to entrench its power permanently.

There’s also a scientific contribution. You don’t have to be working at the company training the largest model to do valuable research on AI safety. We need people investigating how to make systems more understandable, how to evaluate their dangerous capabilities, and how to design them so that they don’t become autonomous agents pursuing power.

Of course, those countries also have to look at their own institutions. Being outside the US and China doesn’t automatically make a government trustworthy. The objective should be to protect democracy and human rights, with checks on power that apply to everyone. I think a coalition built around those principles could make a real difference.

r001.rationale: It says people outside the US and China have an important role and describes how countries can work together to counter concentrated AI power.

r002.rationale: It advocates several actions, but does not communicate that they should be taken despite uncertainty about whether they will help.
